steps.say: Healthy babies spit up frequently because their lower oesophageal sphincter is still maturing. Spitting up reaches its highest peak at four months of age, when over half of all infants regurgitate daily. You can tell the family that it clears up by twelve to fourteen months without any medication.
steps.tx: Observe **physiologic gastroesophageal regurgitation peak** at 4 months of age, affecting over 50% of healthy thriving infants. This effortless regurgitation represents normal physiological development and spontaneously resolves by 12-14 months of age as sphincter tone matures, solid feeds begin, and the child maintains an upright posture.

rows: Over 50% spit up daily; happy spitter with normal growth
Spontaneous resolution in vast majority; no therapy needed

steps.say: Draw a firm line between effortless spitting up and true reflux disease. We only diagnose gastroesophageal reflux disease when reflux causes distressing complications like failure to thrive, hematemesis, food refusal, or aspiration. The happy spitter who gains weight steadily needs reassurance, not acid suppression.
steps.tx: Maintain the **GER vs GERD distinction** strictly under ESPGHAN/NASPGHAN guidelines. Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is diagnosed only when reflux of gastric contents leads to troublesome symptoms or objective complications such as failure to thrive, erosive esophagitis, stricture, or chronic respiratory morbidity. Uncomplicated regurgitation in a thriving child requires no drug intervention.

vis.alt: Refluxed gastric contents injuring the oesophagus and causing complications.
vis.caption: Reflux injures the oesophagus when it becomes disease. Credit: StewardMD.

steps.say: Start with non drug measures before reaching for any prescription pad. Thicken formula feeds using carob or cereal, reduce meal volume while feeding more often, and keep the baby upright for half an hour after feeding. Remember that prone sleeping carries a fatal cot death risk and is strictly forbidden.
steps.tx: Implement **conservative first-line measures** before initiating pharmacotherapy. Recommended adjustments include thickened feeds (using cereal or commercial thickening agents), smaller frequent feedings, and holding the infant upright for 20-30 minutes postprandially. Prone sleeping is strictly contraindicated due to the well-documented risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

nodes.label: Thicken feeds and reduce meal volume
Strict supine sleep to prevent SIDS

steps.say: Spitting up with fussiness often stems from cow milk allergy rather than simple acid reflux. In breastfed infants, eliminate dairy from the mother's diet for two to four weeks. In formula fed babies, switch to an extensively hydrolysed formula for the same trial period before considering acid blocking drugs.
steps.tx: Prescribe a **cow milk protein exclusion trial** for 2 to 4 weeks before initiating acid suppression. Maternal elimination of dairy proteins in breastfed infants, or switching formula-fed infants to an extensively hydrolyzed formula, resolves symptoms in up to a third of infants whose presentation mimics severe gastroesophageal reflux disease.

steps.say: Watch for sudden bizarre neck arching and head turning that occurs during or right after feeding. This is Sandifer syndrome, where the infant stretches the neck to clear acid from the lower oesophagus. It looks exactly like an epileptic seizure, but an electroencephalogram will be completely normal.
steps.tx: Recognise **Sandifer syndrome** as paroxysmal dystonic neck extension and head cocking occurring in temporal association with feeding. This neurobehavioral posturing relieves lower esophageal discomfort by stretching the esophagus and clearing acid, but is frequently misdiagnosed as infantile spasms or focal seizures despite a normal ictal EEG.

nodes.label: Paroxysmal neck arching and head cocking
Posturing clears refluxate from distal lumen

steps.say: When endoscopy confirms mucosal breaks or erosive esophagitis, give a proton pump inhibitor such as omeprazole or esomeprazole at one milligram per kilogram daily. You should keep this course to four to eight weeks, then taper carefully because long term acid suppression invites enteric infections and pneumonia.
steps.tx: Adhere to the **proton pump inhibitor trial duration** guidelines. For endoscopic erosive esophagitis or severe documented reflux disease, administer omeprazole or esomeprazole at 1 mg/kg/day (divided once or twice daily) for a definite course of 4 to 8 weeks. Discontinue or wean therapy thereafter, as prolonged unmonitored use increases vulnerability to gastroenteritis and respiratory infections.

rows: 4 to 8 week course with scheduled taper

steps.say: When symptoms persist despite medical therapy, dual impedance and acidity monitoring gives the complete physiological picture. A slender catheter records electrical impedance across multiple rings to detect bolus transit alongside hydrogen ion changes, catching non acidic reflux that classic pH probes miss completely.
steps.tx: Select **combined pH-impedance monitoring** as the gold standard investigation. Multichannel intraluminal impedance with pH monitoring (MII-pH) detects both acidic (refluxate with pH < 4) and weakly acidic or non-acidic episodes, correlating symptom index and symptom association probability directly with bolus movement along the esophageal body.

left.title: Classic pH Monitoring Alone
points: Detects only acidic events where pH < 4
Cannot measure physical fluid bolus height

right.title: Combined MII-pH Study
points: Detects all refluxate regardless of pH
Quantifies bolus height and clearance time

steps.say: Resist the urge to prescribe prokinetic drugs for childhood reflux. Metoclopramide causes irreversible movement disorders and extrapyramidal reactions, while domperidone can prolong the QT interval and cause fatal arrhythmias. Their safety risks clearly outweigh any minor benefit on gastric emptying.
steps.tx: Avoid routine prokinetics due to **prokinetic drug risks**. Neither metoclopramide nor domperidone is recommended for routine pediatric reflux management. Metoclopramide crosses the blood-brain barrier triggering oculogyric crises and extrapyramidal reactions, while domperidone carries significant cardiac QT prolongation risks without showing reliable mucosal healing.

vis.caption: Prokinetics act on dopamine receptors and carry risks. Credit: StewardMD.
